{{short description|Example of topological space}}
{{distinguish|Line with two origins}}
In mathematics, more specifically [[general topology]], the '''double origin topology''' is an example of a [[topology]] given to the plane {{math|'''R'''{{sup|2}}}} with an extra point, say {{math|0*}}, added. In this case, the double origin topology gives a topology on the set {{math|1=''X'' = '''R'''<sup>2</sup> ⊔ {0*} }}, where {{math|⊔}} denotes the [[disjoint union]].

== Construction ==

Given a point {{mvar|x}} belonging to {{mvar|X}}, such that {{math|1=''x'' ≠ 0}} and {{math|1=''x'' ≠ 0*}}, the [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]]s of {{mvar|x}} are those given by the standard [[metric topology]] on {{math|1='''R'''{{sup|2}}−{0}.}}<ref name="CEIT2">{{Citation|first1=L. A.|last1=Steen|first2=J. A.|last2=Seebach|title=[[Counterexamples in Topology]]|pages=92 − 93|publisher=Dover|year=1995|isbn=0-486-68735-X}}</ref> We define a [[countably infinite]] [[Base (topology)|basis]] of neighbourhoods about the point 0 and about the additional point {{math|0*}}. For the point {{math|0}}, the basis, [[Indexed family|indexed]] by {{mvar|n}}, is defined to be:<ref name="CEIT2"/>
:<math> \ N(0,n) = \{ (x,y) \in {\mathbf R}^2 : x^2 + y^2  < 1/n^2, \ y > 0\} \cup \{0\} . </math>
In a similar way, the basis of neighbourhoods of {{mvar|0*}} is defined to be:<ref name="CEIT2"/>
:<math>N(0^*,n) = \{ (x,y) \in {\mathbf R}^2 : x^2 + y^2  < 1/n^2, \ y < 0\} \cup \{0^*\} . </math>

== Properties ==

The space {{math|1='''R'''<sup>2</sup> ⊔ {{brace|0*}}}}, along with the double origin topology is an example of a [[Hausdorff space]], although it is not [[completely Hausdorff]]. Since it has a base of 
[[Regular open set|regular open sets]], it is an example of a [[semiregular space]] that is not [[Regular space|regular]].  In terms of compactness, the space {{math|1='''R'''<sup>2</sup> ⊔ {{brace|0*}}}}, along with the double origin topology fails to be either [[compact (topology)|compact]], [[paracompact]] or [[locally compact]], however, {{mvar|X}} is [[second countable]]. Finally, it is an example of an [[Connected space#Arc connectedness|arc connected]] space.<ref name="CEIT3">{{Citation|first1=L. A.|last1=Steen|first2=J. A.|last2=Seebach|title=[[Counterexamples in Topology]]|pages=198–199|publisher=Dover|year=1995|isbn=0-486-68735-X}}</ref>
